items.excerpt: 02 November 2026• Update: 02 November 2026 ISTANBUL Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start your Monday, including acting President Iliana Yotova’s victory in Bulgaria’s presidential runoff, a multi-day ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv in the Russian-controlled Ukrainian city of Oleshky ending with no violations, US President Donald Trump prioritizing diplomatic engagement with Iran despite pressure from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to launch military strikes immediately after Tuesday's US midterm elections, and the arrest of more than 200 people in Germany following Gen Z protests. Bulgaria’s acting President Iliana Yotova was heading for a decisive victory in a presidential runoff against her pro-Western challenger, according to exit polls. Completed parallel counts by five major polling agencies put Yotova’s share of the vote at between 56.6% and 58.2% compared with 38.6% to 40.6% for Andrey Gyurov. “We accept the results, no matter how surprising they are,” Gyurov told a press conference in Sofia, adding that while the campaign is ending, the responsibility is not. Yotova, a longtime figure within the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP), improved on her first-round result from last weekend, when she finished with 34.76% against Gyurov at 31.95%. Her campaign emphasized no additional arms support for Ukraine and instead called for peace through a diplomatic solution, in contrast to her rival. - Oleshky ceasefire between Russia, Ukraine ends with no violations reported A multi-day ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv in the Russian-controlled Ukrainian city of Oleshky ended late Sunday with no violations reported by either side. The truce, announced by US first lady Melania Trump to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations, took effect Tuesday and was extended beyond Oleshky, in the Kherson region, to provide safe passage for humanitarian convoys. Trump said the ceasefire had given residents the freedom to move and access to food, clean water, and medicine, as well as "a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack." “Let Oleshky become the starting point for lasting peace,” she wrote on US social media platform X. - Trump favors diplomacy with Iran as Netanyahu urges strikes immediately after Tuesday's US midterms: Report US President Donald Trump is prioritizing diplomatic engagement with Iran despite pressure from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to launch military strikes immediately after Tuesday's US midterm elections, the Axios news site reported Sunday. In a phone conversation Saturday, the Israeli leader pressed Washington to resume military action against Iran shortly after the ballot, but Trump favored allowing ongoing diplomatic tracks to play out, according to American and Israeli sources familiar with the exchange. Netanyahu is concerned about Trump’s approach, according to sources. An Israeli source characterized the discussion as "tough," while a US source described it as "direct." Trump confirmed Sunday that he had spoken with Netanyahu by phone, describing the conversation as “a very good talk.” He said the two discussed Iran but offered no further details. - More than 200 arrests in Germany after Gen Z protests German police arrested more than 200 people after violent clashes erupted in several cities following largely peaceful Generation Z demonstrations demanding better education funding and social policies. The unrest broke out in Hamburg, Frankfurt and Berlin after radical groups staged smaller demonstrations, erecting barricades and clashing with police. The main daytime demonstrations, organized by the Gen Z Regelt initiative across more than 30 cities, brought tens of thousands of young people into the streets to demand greater investment in education, action to ease the rising cost of living and an end to plans to reinstate compulsory military service. After dark, radical groups staged smaller demonstrations in other parts of the cities, erecting barricades as the situation escalated once police moved to contain them. Some activists threw stones, bottles and firecrackers at officers, who responded with water cannons and special units in several locations. ... - Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest F1 world champion with 3rd-place finish in Mexico Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli became the youngest world champion in Formula 1 history, securing the 2026 drivers' title with a third-place finish at the Mexico City Grand Prix. The 20-year-old Italian, who replaced seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton at Mercedes in 2025, claimed his maiden championship in only his second Formula 1 season, with four rounds remaining. Antonelli broke Sebastian Vettel's record as the youngest Formula 1 world champion and became the first Italian to win the drivers' title since Alberto Ascari in 1953. Red Bull's Max Verstappen won the 71-lap race at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, while Ferrari's Hamilton finished second ahead of Antonelli.

President Isaac Herzog, who will begin consultations with parties on Wednesday, has urged politicians to approach negotiations with an open heart and find creative solutions to avoid another election. Eisenkot has since indicated willingness to work with representatives who accept four conditions covering Israeli sovereignty, military service and opposition to Hamas. Morocco welcomed the mission’s closure, while the Polisario and its principal backer, Algeria, condemned the decision. items.title: U.S. Economy Grows 3.4% as 3.7% Inflation Keeps Costs in Focus | EconoTimes
items.excerpt: By Adrian Vale Nov 2, 2026, 4:15 AM UTC Updated Nov 2, 2026, 4:15 AM UTC 3 min read ... The U.S. economy expanded at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, while inflation reached 3.7% over the year through September as voters prepared to weigh economic conditions in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Gallup found that 50% of registered voters surveyed Oct. 1-19 viewed the economy as extremely important to their congressional vote; 42% said the same of gas prices. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted Aug. 28-31, 47% selected cost of living as the single most important factor in their midterm vote. A September AP-NORC survey of 2,140 adults found 17% approved of President Donald Trump’s handling of cost of living and 26% approved of his handling of the economy. The poll’s margin of sampling error was 2.9 percentage points. The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) estimated real gross domestic product (GDP) grew at a 3.4% annual rate from July through September, compared with 2.2% in the second quarter. Investment, consumer spending and government spending contributed to the gain; lower exports partly offset it as imports increased. BEA data show real personal consumption expenditures grew at a 3.8% annual rate. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.6% in September from August and 3.7% over the 12 months through September. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, increased 0.3% for the month and 2.6% over the year. The CPI gasoline index climbed 9.1% in September, accounting for more than half of that month’s increase in the overall index. Annual inflation had fallen from 9.1% in June 2022 to 2.3% in April 2025 before rising again; the lower rate meant prices were rising more slowly, not falling overall. The Conference Board’s Consumer Confidence Index rose 7.5 points to 91.7 in October, from 84.2 in September. The board said confidence remained on a long-term downward trend and consumers planned to reduce spending on services and durable goods over the next six months. Its six-month moving average rose only among consumers younger than 35 and households with incomes of $100,000 or more. Fergus McCormick, a senior economist for Global Indicators at The Conference Board, said consumers “continued to express frustration with rising costs.” AAA’s national averages on Nov. 1 were $4.1732 per gallon for regular gasoline and $6.3039 for diesel, compared with $3.0380 and $3.6862 a year earlier. Freddie Mac reported a 7.24% average rate for a 30-year fixed mortgage on Oct. 29, up from 6.17% on Oct. 30, 2025. The Federal Reserve raised its target range for the federal funds rate by a quarter percentage point in September, then held it at 3.75%-4.00% on Oct. 28; two members favored another increase at that meeting. The S&P 500 closed at 7,580.07 on Oct. 30, below its 7,818.93 close on Oct. 6 but about 10.7% above its Dec. 31, 2025, close of 6,845.50. The next scheduled readings are October CPI on Nov. 10 at 8:30 a.m. ET and the second estimate of third-quarter GDP on Nov. 25 at 8:30 a.m. ET. The Federal Reserve’s next meeting is Dec. 8-9.

items.excerpt: Published Mon, Nov 2 2026 12:04 AM EST ... - U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that Trump prefers not to use military force and would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically." - Iranian ... Oil fell Monday amid news that both the U.S. and Iran seek diplomatic options to their conflict. Futures for international benchmark Brent crude Add To Watchlist for January delivery fell 3.31% to $109.67 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures Add To Watchlist for December declined 3.34% to $100.64 per barrel. ... U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that President Donald Trump prefers not to use military force and would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically." Trump "hasn't made a decision...what the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it, and we really we have everything we need to be successful. But we would prefer to do it peacefully," Rubio said, speaking to reporters over the weekend. Iranian authorities also signaled that a deal is still possible, following two days of talks mediated by Qatar, as long as demands are implemented tangibly, according to Al Jazeera.

items.title: US economy under Donald Trump in five charts | The National
items.excerpt: November 02, 2026 ... Half of registered voters rate the economy as “extremely important this year”, with health care costs and the war in Iran also top among 11 issues rated in an October 29 Gallup poll. Roughly four in 10 voters rate income and wealth distribution (44 per cent) and petrol costs (42 per cent) as extremely important. ... But inflation picked up again after he imposed a sweeping set of tariffs on nearly every trading partner. The disinflation process now appears stalled, and the Iran war has led to surging energy prices couple with AI-driven investment. Petrol prices accounted for nearly half of the all-items increase in September, when CPI inflation clocked in at 3.7 per cent. Even after stripping away food and energy, inflation still gained 0.3 per cent on a monthly basis and 2.6 per cent year on year. It has been nearly six years since CPI inflation registered at 2 per cent. Seventy-nine per cent of Americans agreed that prices at the pump were higher now compared to 38 per cent in February, a dramatic shift in perceptions since the Iran war began, according to an Ipsos poll conducted in September. The prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the world's energy supplies, has pushed up global energy costs. Even the US, the world's top crude producer, has not been fully insulated. Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries have exacerbated rising costs for diesel, which powers the lorries that transport food and other goods. The average driver is currently paying $4.20 for a gallon of petrol today, an increase of $1.17 from the same time last year, according to automotive group AAA. Of the six “swing states” in this year's midterm election cycle, only Georgia's petrol prices are below the national average. Diesel prices have also soared to $6.32, compared to $3.68 a gallon a year ago.

items.title: Dollar Index Holds Near 102 as Inflation and Iran Diplomacy Shape Trading | EconoTimes
items.excerpt: The U.S. Dollar Index (DXY) was near 102 in Asian trading Monday, FXStreet reported, as September inflation and Iran diplomacy shaped competing pressures on the U.S. currency. FXStreet said waning demand for the dollar’s safe-haven role was restraining it; the outlet also cited inflation and rate-hike expectations as offsetting forces. ... The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) reported that the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose 0.5% from August and 3.6% from a year earlier in September, compared with increases of 0.3% and 3.4% in August. Core PCE advanced 0.3% month over month and 3.1% year over year, after increases of 0.3% and 3.0% in August. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% on Oct. 28. The 10-2 vote included two officials who favored a 0.25-percentage-point increase. The committee said, “Inflation remains elevated.” FXStreet reported roughly 75% odds of a December increase, citing CME FedWatch. CME says its probabilities are implied by 30-Day Federal Funds futures prices.

items.title: Trump makes final weekend campaign push ahead of midterm elections
items.excerpt: In the last weekend before the pivotal midterm elections, Donald Trump has made a final pitch to voters in hopes of keeping Republicans in control of the US Congress. Trump held rallies in Florida, Iowa and Kansas - states he won in past elections - in a sign of Republicans' defensive stance in Tuesday's elections. Facing voter frustration over rising prices, particularly fuel, Trump sought to tamp down such concerns and shift focus on attacking Democrats, saying they would "bankrupt" families if elected. Polls suggest that Democrats have a good chance at winning at least partial control of Congress, which would act as a check on Trump's power and upend the last two years of his presidency. ... Trump is facing a backlash over the cost of living. Prices have gone up, particularly for fuel, groceries and health care, since the war in Iran began over eight months ago. At these rallies, Trump appeared to have two aims: to change the subject from those issues and use fear to turn out the Republican vote. ... In the room at the rallies, supporters cheered, but there has also been disquiet among some Republicans over Trump's appeal with more moderate voters. Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries said this weekend that he was "very confident" his party was on course to win control of the House of Representatives, as senior Democrats including former President Barack Obama made final appeals to voters. A forecasting tool from Harvard University that analyses and compiles multiple polls and historical data suggests that Democrats have a 96% chance of taking the House and a 76% chance of taking the Senate. A national poll from NBC News posted this weekend suggests that registered voters prefer a Democrat-controlled Congress by a 7-point margin, leading Republicans 52% to 45%. But along with the last-push campaign stops, this weekend featured a dramatic turn in the Senate race in Michigan - a tightly contested seat currently held by Democrats.

items.title: Trump leans into Islamophobia and conspiracy in last-ditch campaign rallies | US Midterm Elections 2026 News | Al Jazeera
items.excerpt: United States President Donald Trump has doubled down on Islamophobic rhetoric and conspiracy theories about the Democratic Party at campaign events in Iowa and Kansas, days before the US votes in crucial midterm elections that will decide who controls Congress during Trump’s last two years as president. The president repeated his claim that Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic US Senate hopeful from Michigan, is a “jihadist” at both rallies on Sunday, and joked that if he gets elected, the Senate will have to install metal detectors to scan him before he enters the building. “We’ll have a hundred senators, and most of them will go directly [into the Senate]… We’re gonna have to get a special metal detector for Abdul,” Trump said, drawing laughter from the crowd. He also repeated unfounded claims that El-Sayed is a member of the transnational Muslim Brotherhood, branches of which the US has deemed foreign “terrorist” organisations. At both events, Trump repeatedly urged his supporters to make sure they go out and vote, asking them to “pretend I’m on the ballot”, as he sought to energise Republican voters ahead of what polling suggests could be a bruising election for the party. The two rallies were cancelled last week but were suddenly rescheduled. They will be Trump’s final travelling events before the election. ... In Kansas, Trump attacked the Democratic Senate hopeful Adam Hamilton, a church pastor, for his support for trans rights, and called him a “stiff” who reads his sermons from teleprompters.

items.title: AP News in Brief at 12:04 a.m. EST | 10tv.com
items.excerpt: Published: 12:00 AM EST November 2, 2026 Updated: 12:04 AM EST November 2, 2026 Judge dismisses lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska Senate race if GOP incumbent loses JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — A federal judge on Sunday dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses, the latest development in a ballot controversy that has roiled the final days of one of the nation’s most closely watched races. Sullivan, an ally of President Donald Trump, faces Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, in a race that is among a handful expected to determine which party controls the Senate for the final two years of Trump's term. Tuesday’s ranked-choice election also includes two candidates who have done little campaigning, one of whom shares the incumbent’s name. It was that candidate's presence on the ballot that prompted Trump to push for the lawsuit out of fear he would siphon votes from the incumbent. Shortly after the ruling, the Justice Department filed a notice that it would appeal: “Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” a department spokesperson said in a statement. The lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before the election and as early voting was underway, called for an investigation into whether votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan were intended for the senator. The state said the case lacked merit and argued there would be no way to determine that without violating voter privacy. Analysis: Republicans face a midterm reckoning of Trump's making WASHINGTON (AP) — For President Donald Trump, this week's elections are about him. For his fellow Republicans, the risk is voters will agree. Midterms almost always serve as a referendum on the president’s party, and losses typically ensue. But Trump’s decisions to impose tariffs, start a war and oversee extravagant Washington renovations — largely without congressional consultation — have made it harder for Republicans to navigate those historical headwinds. There is a direct connection between his actions and higher gas prices, costlier groceries and persistently high inflation. Republicans cannot blame the fallout from those decisions on past administrations when Trump has owned them so fulsomely. They also cannot easily distance themselves from an unpopular president who demands loyalty and routinely tells voters the economy is just fine. At virtually every juncture before Election Day on Tuesday, Trump has complicated the task of protecting Republican majorities in Congress.

items.title: US midterm elections could see key demographics that ...
items.excerpt: US President Donald Trump was catapulted to the White House for a second term by a diverse, working-class coalition. Many people in this powerful bloc, from gen Z men to Latinos and evangelical Christians, backed the president's America First agenda in 2024. But two years into his second term, his approval ratings have plummeted and there are signs his support in these groups is crumbling. While the president's personal brand is still considered strong among his MAGA base, Mr Trump's name will not appear on any ballots at the US midterm elections this week. The ABC spoke to several voters from key demographics who backed Mr Trump last time, to see whether his Republican Party would get their support on Tuesday, local time, or whether they had changed their minds. ... Mr Trump made significant gains among Latino voters in 2024, with multiple polls indicating his support increased from 32 per cent at the 2020 presidential election to 48 per cent four years later. But there are indications of a massive reversal now, with a recent New York Times/Sienna poll giving Democrats a 30-point lead among the diverse voting bloc.

A data breach at the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) exposed information from applications for more than 500 titles, dozens of which were feature films, The Hindu found. The leak appears to have originated from the e-Cinepramaan portal, launched nearly a decade ago to digitise the CBFC’s work. items.title: Anirudh exits Shah Rukh Khan's King, Sachin-Jigar take over music duties - India Today
items.excerpt: New Delhi, Nov 2, 2026 10:42 IST It's now clear that Shah Rukh Khan's King has a new musical team. Composer-singer Anirudh has reportedly stepped away from the film because of his packed schedule. However, he isn't leaving the project entirely empty-handed. He's said to have given Shah Rukh a theme track as a mark of respect for the actor, even as composer-duo Sachin-Jigar take charge of the film's songs and background score. According to a report by *Bollywood Hungama*, Anirudh and the makers mutually decided to part ways after his commitments in the South made it difficult for him to give the film the time it needed. With Shah Rukh and director Siddharth Anand keen to bring *King* to cinemas this Christmas without delays, the team reportedly decided to make the change. ... The decision to part ways from the project was reportedly amicable, with Sachin-Jigar now handling the album as well as the background score. Anirudh, meanwhile, has composed the film's theme track, which will continue to feature in the project. ... ### SRK- Deepika Padukone's *Tu Mil Jaaye* releases The timing is interesting, as *King* has just begun unveiling its music. Shah Rukh marked his birthday on November 2 with the midnight release of *Tu Mil Jaaye*, the film's first song, which features him alongside Deepika Padukone. The track has received mixed reactions. While Arijit Singh's vocals, the melody and Shah Rukh and Deepika's chemistry have found appreciation, some listeners have questioned its familiar sound, visuals, editing and styling. Ed Sheeran's English rap has also become a talking point, with comparisons being drawn to songs from Siddharth's earlier films, including Pathaan. Composed by Sachin-Jigar, *Tu Mil Jaaye* features vocals by Arijit Singh and Madhubanti Bagchi, with Sheeran performing the English rap. The romantic track also brings Shah Rukh and Deepika together on screen once again.
